name: Postural Integration

image.caption: Dr. Jack Painter, Postural Integration process-oriented body-based therapy

lead: Postural Integration is a bodywork method devised by Jack Painter in California in the late 1960s, combining deep tissue massage, breathwork and Gestalt-style awareness. It is loosely modelled on Rolfing and typically runs as a twelve-session course.
For looks, the appeal is posture: practitioners say releasing chronic muscular tension changes how a person stands, moves and carries themselves, which shows as a more open, upright frame.

paras: A course is usually delivered as twelve sessions, the first seven working through body areas to release what practitioners call defensive 'armoring'. Sessions combine hands-on work, breathing and attention to emotion and body language.

Risks are those of deep manual work and emotional release, such as soreness. Wikipedia notes no controlled studies of effectiveness for the original method, and critics such as Quackwatch characterise its energy claims as alleged.

angle.text: Practitioners say the sessions loosen chronic tension so the body is carried more easily. Any change in look comes through posture rather than a direct physical alteration.

lead: Postural Integration is a bodywork method developed by Jack Painter (1933 to 2010), a former philosophy professor at the University of Miami, in California in the late 1960s. It drew on humanistic psychology and the human potential movement, and on Rolfing, Gestalt therapy and Wilhelm Reich's vegetotherapy.[1]

A typical course is twelve sessions loosely modelled on Rolfing, combining bodywork, breathwork, Gestalt therapy, 'fine energy' work and elements of the Five Phases system. The first seven sessions target body areas to release defensive armoring.[1]

Posture is a visible part of appearance, which is why such methods appear in self-improvement circles: proponents say less muscular holding leads to a more natural, upright stance. A separate physiotherapy technique abbreviated PIMT (Postural Integration by Manual Therapy) has been tested in a small trial on hindfoot valgus.[2]

paras: Painter explored massage, acupuncture, Zen, yoga, Rolfing, Gestalt therapy and Reichian work before calling his approach Postural Integration in the 1970s; he later developed Energetic Integration and Pelvic-Heart Integration.[1] Spontaneous emotional expression is encouraged, and some practitioners emphasise psychotherapy while others use it mainly as bodywork. A 1990s offshoot, Psychotherapeutic Postural Integration, added Jungian psychology.[1]

Wikipedia, citing Quackwatch, describes the method as aiming at 'access to the past' and release of energy toward a 'light, joyful balance'. Practitioners present it as freeing the body from defensive tension.[1]

No controlled studies of Painter's Postural Integration are cited in reference sources.[1] A separate study of PIMT (Postural Integration by Manual Therapy) compared it with Global Postural Reeducation in 60 Brazilian Army subjects with hindfoot valgus, over four weekly sessions. Both improved body-weight load symmetry equally, and plantar surface symmetry was better in the PIMT group four weeks later.[2] That technique is a physiotherapy procedure and not necessarily the same method.
